title: De insigni paradoxo, quod in analysi maximorum et minimorum occurrit

deep.reconstruction:
Euler continues the 'paradox' paper of 1779. He takes the horizontal line AB as reference and a vertical axis AC. For a point Y of the sought curve EY, the abscissa is AX = x, which equals the depth YV of Y below AB, and the ordinate is XY = y. With dy = p dx, the arc element is ds = dx√(1+p²). The functional to be minimised, the sum of the arc elements each multiplied by √(depth), is J[y] = ∫ √x · √(1+p²) dx.

§3 gives a mechanical reading. A body falling from rest at the level of AB has speed v ∝ √x at depth x. So J = ∫ v ds, which is Maupertuis' action (Euler cites his own earlier observation, i.e. the 1744 Additamentum II to the Methodus inveniendi). By the least-action principle the extremals are therefore free-fall trajectories with total energy fixed so that the speed vanishes on AB. These are parabolas with vertical axes. Implicitly AB is their common directrix, which is confirmed on the next page: the vertex distance to AB equals the focal distance.

§4 begins the analytic route. Compare J with Euler's general form ∫V dx, where dV = M dx + N dy + P dp. The Euler equation N dx = dP follows on the next page, with N = 0 giving a first integral P = const. This yields p√x/√(1+p²) = √a, hence y = 2√(ax − a²) + b.

The page only sets up the problem whose 'paradox' is developed later. Pairs of endpoints may admit two, one or no such parabolas (the envelope is the 'parabola of safety'). Competing broken curves can also do better, e.g. rising vertically to AB, running along AB at zero cost, and descending again.
errors: No error on this page. The identification of the extremals with projectile paths rests on the (Jacobi-form) least-action principle with energy fixed by the speed vanishing at AB. Euler tacitly assumes this, and it is correct. 'Minimum' is asserted for extremals without any sufficiency analysis; that gap is precisely the subject of the paradox.

ideas.what: Minimising ∫√x ds, i.e. a weighted-length (optical/Jacobi-metric) problem with index √x
ideas.modern_name: Jacobi metric / geodesics of the Maupertuis action for uniform gravity
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jacobi (1837/1842) for the metric formulation; Euler 1744 for least action in this form

ideas.what: Identification of the extremals with projectile parabolas sharing the directrix AB (the level of zero velocity)
ideas.modern_name: Energy-shell trajectories; the common directrix as the zero-kinetic-energy line
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Galileo for parabolic trajectories; Euler for the least-action derivation)
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum II; this paper E735

ideas.what: Using the general form ∫V dx with dV = M dx + N dy + P dp and the equation N dx = dP; first integral when N = 0

missed.claim: The paradox set up here, where extremals fail to minimise or fail to exist between given endpoints, is an early concrete instance of what Jacobi's conjugate-point theory and Weierstrass/Goldschmidt-type broken minimisers later explained. Here it is tied to the envelope of projectile trajectories (the parabola of safety). This page only states the setup, so the substantive content lies on later pages; the historiography (e.g. Goldstine, Fraser) may already discuss it — unsure.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a historical priority/context point for the second-variation theory. It is mathematically known today.

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the routine setup of a published paper. The least-action identification is Euler's own known 1744 result, and the deeper conjugate-point anticipation belongs to the following pages and is plausibly already noted by historians.
